items.followUp: Define a saturated solution and give one example.

rubric.why: Aqueous solutions are homogeneous mixtures in which water is the solvent.
rubric.description: Defines an aqueous solution as a homogeneous mixture with water as the solvent.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying water as the solvent in a homogeneous solution.

rubric.why: A suitable example shows a substance dissolved in water.
rubric.description: Gives a suitable example, such as salt or sugar dissolved in water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct example.

modelAnswer: An aqueous solution is a homogeneous mixture in which water is the solvent.
For example, sodium chloride dissolved in water forms an aqueous solution.

items.followUp: Why can a beam of light be seen when it passes through a colloid?

rubric.why: Scattering of light by colloidal particles is the cause of the Tyndall effect.
rubric.description: States that colloidal particles scatter light.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying light scattering by the particles.

rubric.why: The scattered light makes the path of the beam visible.
rubric.description: Explains that scattering makes the beam's path visible.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking scattering to the visible path of light.

modelAnswer: Colloidal particles scatter the light passing through a colloid.
The scattered light makes the path of the beam visible; this is called the Tyndall effect.

items.followUp: Define a weak electrolyte and give one example.

rubric.why: A strong electrolyte produces ions almost completely in solution or in the molten state.
rubric.description: States that a strong electrolyte ionizes or dissociates completely.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for complete ionization or dissociation.

rubric.why: The ions produced carry electric charge through the solution or melt.
rubric.description: States that it conducts electricity well or gives a correct example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for electrical conduction or an appropriate example such as NaCl or HCl.

modelAnswer: A strong electrolyte is a substance that ionizes almost completely in aqueous solution or in the molten state.
It conducts electricity well; for example, sodium chloride (NaCl) is a strong electrolyte.

items.followUp: Why do metals lose electrons when forming ions?

rubric.why: Non-metals tend to gain electrons in chemical reactions.
rubric.description: States that non-metals gain or accept electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying electron gain.

rubric.why: Gaining electrons helps non-metals attain a stable outer shell like that of a noble gas.
rubric.description: Explains that gaining electrons completes the outer shell or gives a stable configuration.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the stability or complete-shell reason.

modelAnswer: Non-metals accept electrons to complete their outermost shell.
This gives them a stable electronic configuration like that of a noble gas.

items.followUp: Write the chemical formula of magnesium chloride by using the valencies of its ions.

rubric.why: The formula begins with the correct symbols for the elements or ions in the compound.
rubric.description: Writes the correct symbols of the constituent elements or ions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly identifying and writing the symbols.

rubric.why: Valencies are needed to determine the subscripts in the formula.
rubric.description: Identifies or writes the valencies of the constituent elements or ions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating or correctly using the valencies.

rubric.why: Interchanging the valencies gives the initial subscripts.
rubric.description: Explains the interchange (criss-cross) of valencies to form subscripts.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct valency-interchange method.

rubric.why: Subscripts must be reduced to the simplest whole-number ratio where possible.
rubric.description: Reduces the subscripts to the simplest whole-number ratio.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating or applying reduction of subscripts.

rubric.why: A worked example demonstrates the formula-writing method, including correct final subscripts.
rubric.description: Gives a correct example of the method, such as CaCl₂ or Al₂O₃.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correctly formed example formula.

modelAnswer: Write the symbols of the elements or ions in the compound: Ca and Cl.
Write their valencies: Ca = 2 and Cl = 1.
Interchange the valencies and write them as subscripts: Ca₁Cl₂.
Reduce the subscripts to the simplest whole-number ratio, if possible.
Omit the subscript 1; therefore, the formula of calcium chloride is CaCl₂.

items.followUp: Define an ionic bond and describe how it forms in sodium chloride.

rubric.why: A covalent bond forms through the sharing of electron pairs between atoms.
rubric.description: Defines a covalent bond as a bond formed by sharing electron pairs.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the sharing-of-electrons definition.

rubric.why: One shared pair of electrons forms a single covalent bond.
rubric.description: Identifies a single covalent bond as one shared pair of electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the single-bond type and its shared-pair count.

rubric.why: Two shared pairs form a double covalent bond.
rubric.description: Identifies a double covalent bond as two shared pairs of electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the double-bond type and its shared-pair count.

rubric.why: Three shared pairs form a triple covalent bond.
rubric.description: Identifies a triple covalent bond as three shared pairs of electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the triple-bond type and its shared-pair count.

modelAnswer: A covalent bond is formed when atoms share one or more pairs of electrons.
A single covalent bond involves one shared pair, for example, in H₂.
A double covalent bond involves two shared pairs, for example, in O₂.
A triple covalent bond involves three shared pairs, for example, in N₂.

items.followUp: What are anode rays? Write four properties of anode rays.

rubric.why: Cathode rays are streams of electrons emitted from the cathode in a discharge tube.
rubric.description: Defines cathode rays as streams of electrons or negatively charged particles from the cathode.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying cathode rays as electrons or negatively charged particles.

rubric.why: Cathode rays propagate in straight lines.
rubric.description: Gives the straight-line travel property.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this property.

rubric.why: Their negative charge makes them deflect in electric or magnetic fields, toward the positive plate in an electric field.
rubric.description: States that cathode rays are deflected by an electric or magnetic field, or toward the positive plate.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct deflection property.

rubric.why: Cathode rays cause certain materials to fluoresce when they strike them.
rubric.description: States that cathode rays produce fluorescence.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this property.

rubric.why: Cathode rays have mass and kinetic energy and can produce a heating effect on impact.
rubric.description: Gives another valid property, such as having mass or kinetic energy, or producing heat.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one further correct property.

modelAnswer: Cathode rays are streams of electrons emitted from the cathode in a discharge tube.
They travel in straight lines.
They are deflected by electric and magnetic fields, showing that they are negatively charged.
They produce fluorescence when they strike certain substances.
They possess mass and kinetic energy and can produce a heating effect.

items.followUp: Define melting point and state the melting and boiling points of water at standard atmospheric pressure.

rubric.why: Freezing is the change from liquid to solid; the freezing point is the temperature at which it occurs.
rubric.description: Defines freezing point as the temperature at which a liquid changes into a solid.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct phase change and temperature definition.

rubric.why: Boiling is the change from liquid to gas; the boiling point is the temperature at which it occurs.
rubric.description: Defines boiling point as the temperature at which a liquid changes into a gas.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct phase change and temperature definition.

rubric.why: Water freezes at 0 °C at standard atmospheric pressure.
rubric.description: Gives the freezing point of water as 0 °C.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct example value.

rubric.why: Water boils at 100 °C at standard atmospheric pressure.
rubric.description: Gives the boiling point of water as 100 °C.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct example value.

modelAnswer: The freezing point is the temperature at which a liquid changes into a solid.
The boiling point is the temperature at which a liquid changes into a gas.
For water at standard atmospheric pressure, the freezing point is 0 °C.
At the same pressure, the boiling point of water is 100 °C.
